messages.author: 028f6dd03e1f43b1
messages.subject: Default Colors --
parts:
This should be easy but, if so, I have not found the easy solution — yet.

I allow ggplot2 to specify its default colors for 9 different lines (one for each subject (aka: SID) as in:

geom_line(data=sf.9byHr, aes(x=Hour, y=m.pnts, color=SID), size=1), where each line shows a different subject’s data.

I have some beautiful plots. But now I realize that for presentation purposes, I want to plot a few of the subjects by themselves, e.g.,

geom_line(data=subset(sf.9byHr, SID == "sid1639"), aes(x=Hour, y=m.pnts), size=1)

BUT I now want the color to be the same color as was chosen by ggplot when there were 9 lines.

I just did this the “hard” way by establishing a palette of 9 colors, and using:

scale_colour_manual(values = cbbPalette) to assign colors to subjects. I then assigned each SID the color they were given by cbbPalette — It all worked fine but seems to me too much work with too many steps for too many special cases.

Is there an easier way of assigning one SID the same color in the individual plot as was assigned in the group (9 SIDs) plot while using the default colors?

messages.author: afa3a78132320260
messages.subject: Re: Default Colors --
parts:
Not sure what you are looking for, but here some examples.

If you have nine different lines, we can get the default colors like this:

library(scales)
cols <- hue_pal()(9)

show_col(cols)

To plot, for example, the first subject you can use these colors in the plotting call:
geom_line(data=subset(sf.9byHr, SID == "sid1639"), aes(x=Hour, y=m.pnts), size=1, col = cols[1])
#or directly
geom_line(data=subset(sf.9byHr, SID == "sid1639"), aes(x=Hour, y=m.pnts), size=1, col  = hue_pal()(9)[1])

#or perhaps like this, if SID is a factor:
subject <-"sid1639"
geom_line(data=subset(sf.9byHr, SID == subject), aes(x=Hour, y=m.pnts), size=1, col  = hue_pal()(9)[which(levels(sf.9byHr$SID == subject)])

Alternatively, you can use facetting to create all nine plots with the appropriate scales and colors at once.

Hth,
W.

parts:
Woulter,

Many thanks! That is the info I was searching for.

You are right about faceting (of course) and I was doing that for my inspection, but the next step — printing each out so as to show one per slide — was what drove me to the one-by-one method. However, given how it works (thanks again!), it will be easy to write a function to save each to as a separate pdf.

Wayne

messages.author: f20966e9bc9cf5c7
messages.subject: Re: Default Colors --
parts:
Hello Wayne,

Unsurprisingly, doing this is very elegant.
Please see: http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/scale_manual.html

There you should find an example of what you want to do. I think this
one should work fine:

library(ggplot2)
cols <- c("8" = "red", "4" = "blue", "6" = "darkgreen", "10" = "orange")
ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt, color=factor(cyl))) +
geom_point() +
scale_colour_manual(values = cols)

ggplot(subset(mtcars, cyl == "6"), aes(mpg, wt, color=factor(cyl))) +
geom_point() +
xlim(10, 33) + ylim(1, 5) + # to make the two plots comparable
scale_colour_manual(values = cols)

For publication, it is convenient to define something similar to "cols"
at the start and be done with it - by adding 'scale_colour_manual(values
= cols)'.

Next time you want help with something, please include a reproducible
example.

Cheers,
Brian
